newsitem.title: USA: No revolutionary change for Rolls-Royce.
newsitem.headline: No revolutionary change for Rolls-Royce.

text.p: Rolls-Royce has high hopes for its planned new models but the luxury car maker is not about to make revolutionary design changes, according to chief executive Graham Morris.

The venerable British manufacturer of some of the world's most expensive cars plans to introduce a new Rolls-Royce and Bentley by the turn of the century -- the first completely new models since 1980.

"With the new product we obviously need to take a step forward and that product has to last us into the next century," Morris, chief executive of Rolls-Royce Motor Cars Ltd., said in an interview late (on) Thursday.
Morris said the new Rolls, now in development, would be "more rounded in its shape ... not square like the car today, but still very much a Rolls-Royce."
"It's a nice evolution. Strong marques like Rolls-Royce and Bentley are not in revolutions like the volume manufacturers," he said.
However, Morris said there would be only three carryover parts on the new car. "It's a completely new car," he said. He would not say exactly when the new models will be launched.

The company said last month it sold 1,029 Rolls-Royces and Bentleys in the first half of 1997, a 13 percent increase from a year ago. Morris said the company aimed to increase sales, within a couple of years of the launch of the new models, to about 2,500 cars a year, compared to 1,744 cars in 1996.

Morris was in California for the U.S. launch of the 1998 Bentley Azure convertible at the Concours d'Elegance, a classic car event in Pebble Beach on the central California coast. The Azure is one of the most expensive cars on the company's U.S. price list, retailing for almost $340,000. The cheapest is the Bentley Brooklands, which sells for $155,900.
Morris, who joined Rolls in March from Audi, said Rolls-Royce, a subsidiary of engineering group Vickers Plc, was "entering a new era."
"We're reconstructing the factory ... There are new models on the way ... There are new processes going into the factory and we're trying to instill a new culture," he said.
"We've had to do this really because we need a significant productivity improvement on our new products ...," he said.

Referring to recurring speculation that Vickers could sell Rolls-Royce, Morris said he had stated repeatedly that there were absolutely no discussions going on. "Vickers have made it very clear they want Rolls-Royce to stay part of the company and to remain British," he said.

Asked about the possibility of smaller models, Morris said some believed there was a niche for Bentley "in a slightly smaller form, and I stress slightly smaller form, and again we are not talking about large volumes here."
"There's no plans, no money being spent, there's no models ... I just think as a dream that this is something we could have a look at (in) the future, but it's not for today," he said.
But he said Bentleys and Rolls-Royces would never be cheap because that would undermine the marque. "Our products will always command a premium price and quite rightly," he said.
Morris said Rolls-Royce had to develop its "branded goods potential" -- using the Rolls logos to market other luxury products.

"We are looking at opportunities ... It would be very exclusive high fashion goods, a whole range of goods. It would be primarily exclusive to our customers but the general public could also buy them," he said. The company sold accessories today but "it's nowhere near ... where it should be," he said.
Morris said Rolls' unique selling point was that it could tailor a car to a customer's wishes. The customer could choose different types of carpet, leather and other features.
Half of Rolls-Royces sold had some form of individualization ranging from a few thousand dollars to $50,000 or more, Morris said. "We'd like to get that to 100 percent," he said.
"If you want a complete car built from the ground up that is ... unique for you, then we will do it," he said.

Morris said Rolls-Royces remained a desirable product for the world's super-rich. "It is the only British brand in the top 10 brands in the world from an awareness point of view. It is incredibly strong. Our customers are extremely loyal," he said.
